subject: Wiring lanes: ingress transport options for Acme Analytics (peering | PrivateLink | S2S VPN)
messages:
From: Vivek Kulkarni <vivek@redwood.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>, acme-netops@acme.example.com
Cc: eric.smith@acme.example.com

Subject: Wiring lanes: ingress transport options for Acme Analytics (peering | PrivateLink | S2S VPN)

Team / Acme,

Thanks for joining the short workshop this morning. Attached are the raw decision matrix and the whiteboard snapshot (both attached). I captured the key tradeoffs we discussed and sketched a recommended pilot wiring pattern for Acme Analytics. High-level notes: 

- Goal: low-latency, source-IP-preserving data plane for inference requests from Acme VPCs into our Private deployment while preserving strict egress attribution and least-privilege surface area.
- Constraints: Acme requires per-tenant IP visibility for downstream logging, SOC 2 evidence of separation between control and data planes, and the ability to fall back to a lower-cost path if dedicated paths saturate.

Summary recommendation (pilot): Hybrid approach — use PrivateLink (interface endpoints) for control plane / API management (auth, health-checks, model selection) and a BGP-backed site-to-site VPN (or IPsec) for the bulk data plane for the initial pilot. Rationale: PrivateLink minimizes cross-account route exposure and keeps control plane endpoints private; S2S with BGP preserves source IPs (via routed topology) and provides simpler throughput scaling for large payloads. VPC peering was judged lower priority because of cross-account route table complexity and scaling friction across many Acme subnets.

Open items for decision:
- If Acme prefers source-IP preservation without NAT in all cases, we need to confirm their willingness to accept an S2S-controlled ASN and BGP session (or arrange Direct Connect).
- MTU/fragmentation expectations: benchmarking required for 1MB requests (we saw fragmentation risk in the matrix).
- Monitoring and failover: define RTO for dataplane and implement cold fallback to PrivateLink-based proxied path if BGP link fails.

Action requested: please review the attached matrix and the wiring diagram. Kimberly, can you add the operational runbook rows for interface endpoints vs BGP (route propagation, ephemeral IPs, monitoring hooks)? Connor, can you capture the rollout checklist including canary and rate-limits for the pilot? Marissa, I’ll need a security note for the audit trail (KMS usage, egress logging). Acme: Eric, request your team to confirm whether S2S with BGP is allowed on their side and whether they have a preferred ASN / VPN appliance.

I put a quick mutual action plan in the spreadsheet (tab: MAP). If we can confirm S2S allowance by end of Thursday we can schedule a short pilot cutover window next week.

Subject: Re: Wiring lanes: ingress transport options for Acme Analytics (peering | PrivateLink | S2S VPN)

Thanks — good capture. A few technical clarifications from infra that should be recorded in the matrix (adding inline):

> - MTU/fragmentation expectations: benchmarking required for 1MB requests (we saw fragmentation risk in the matrix).

Note: default ENI MTU on most clouds is 1500; Jumbo frames can help but require coordination. If Acme sends 1MB payloads frequently, we must either (a) enforce chunking at the client, (b) enable jumbo MTU (requires coordination and rarely works across S2S appliances), or (c) tunnel over a transport that supports large payloads (e.g., Direct Connect + path MTU control). For the pilot, assume chunking at the SDK layer unless Acme commits to network changes.

> - Source IP preservation via BGP

We can preserve client source IPs if we accept routed mode with BGP and avoid NAT at the edge. That requires Acme to advertise their subnets to us (or accept our advertised /32s) and for us to propagate routes into our VPCs. Operationally, this increases attack surface for routing — we should include explicit prefix filters and ROA requirements where applicable.

> - PrivateLink for control plane

Operational note: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) gives us per-service ENIs in the customer VPC. It isolates control plane traffic and simplifies DNS. However, PrivateLink does not natively pass arbitrary source IPs — the service side will see the endpoint ENI as the source unless we use proxying inside our private deploy (which then removes source-ip fidelity). That’s why I agree with the hybrid: PrivateLink for control plane, BGP/S2S for data flows where IP fidelity matters.

I’ll add a short runbook tab to the matrix: route filters, ephemeral ENI monitoring, endpoint lifecycle, and a fallback path to proxied PrivateLink in case BGP flaps. Also adding test cases: 100 RPS with 500B payloads, 50 RPS with 1MB payloads, get return-path validation for logging.

-Kimberly

Vivek / Kimberly — thanks for running this. A couple quick clarifying questions from our netops team: 

1) If we do the hybrid you describe, will we need to open any inbound CIDR ranges in our VPC for peering or PrivateLink? What will show up in our route tables?
2) Does the S2S option require us to NAT outbound traffic so that we can correlate requests with a single egress IP? We currently tag logs by source IP at our WAF layer and would prefer minimal transformation.
3) Fallback behavior: if we put PrivateLink in place as the control plane and the BGP link drops, will you be able to accept proxied requests over PrivateLink without losing routing context we use in our auditing?

We can answer ASN and appliance model today — we use Palo Alto PA-DFS with ASA fallback. On the ASN side we prefer to keep our public ASN internal and let you allocate a private ASN for the peer — happy to share details offline.

From: Connor O'Brien <connor_obrien@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Wiring lanes: ingress transport options for Acme Analytics (peering | PrivateLink | S2S VPN)

Eric — good questions. Short answers inline, and then the rollout checklist I'm adding to the sheet: 

1) Route tables / inbound CIDRs: for PrivateLink you get interface ENIs in your subnets — no route-table changes required beyond security group/ENI permissions. For S2S routed mode we'll ask you to accept specific prefixes (we'll provide exact /28s or /32s for the pilot) and enable route propagation on your side. We'll provide the BGP filters so you only learn the small set of prefixes for the pilot.

2) NAT / egress IPs: if you want the original client IP preserved through the data plane, do not NAT at the customer edge. We can preserve it if routes are propagated and we avoid proxy NAT. If your WAF requires a single egress IP for telemetry, we can add SNAT on your side before sending to us, or we can provide a small set of stable egress IPs via a managed NAT gateway on the B side — tradeoff is you lose per-client IP visibility. For auditability, preserve source IPs at the earliest possible hop; we will ingest those into our logs with a signed envelope for later SOC evidence.

3) Fallback: Yes, we can accept proxied requests over PrivateLink if BGP is down, but an important note: you will lose original source-ip fidelity unless we deploy a header-preservation proxy that inserts the original IP in an X-Forwarded-For header, and your audit pipeline accepts that header as authoritative for logs and compliance (we'll sign it). That flow will need to be added to the compliance runbook and tested.

Rollout checklist (high level):
- MUTUAL ACTION: Acme to provide ASN/appliance details + test VPC subnet for POC (Due Thu)
- Redwood: provide BGP prefix filters, ephemeral prefix list, and canary config for traffic shaping (Due Fri)
- Infra test: MTU and chunking scripts, large-payload perf (30m) (Due Mon)
- Security: KMS & logging envelope validation tests (Due Mon)

I updated the spreadsheet with the checkboxes and assigned owners. If everyone is aligned, schedule 1-hour cutover window next Wed for the pilot.
